notes.meaning: Paul compares our physical body to a temporary tent that will one day be taken down. A tent is fragile and easily worn out, but God has prepared a permanent, eternal home in heaven for his people. This heavenly building is the resurrection body that God himself makes. Believers can face death without terror because our future with God is completely secure.

While living in our current bodies, we groan because of sickness, pain, and trials. We do not groan in hopelessness, but because we eagerly long for the glorified body God will give us at Christ's return. We yearn to be clothed with that heavenly home like a permanent, glorious garment.

Paul explains that when Christ gives us our heavenly dwelling, we will not be left naked or without a body. Many ancient Greek philosophers taught that the soul was better off without any physical body at all. The gospel teaches that God made people to have both body and soul, and he will clothe us with a glorious resurrection body.

Believers feel weighed down by the daily hardships and weaknesses of life in a frail body. Paul clarifies that we do not want to escape into nothingness or simply shed our bodies, for dying itself is not our desire. Instead, we want our mortal nature to be swallowed up and transformed by immortal life when Christ returns.

God himself is the one who created and shaped us for this glorious eternal future. To guarantee this promise, he has placed the Holy Spirit in our hearts as a pledge, which is like a down payment on a purchase. The presence and work of the Spirit give us constant assurance that God will bring us into full glory.

Because the Holy Spirit lives within us, we can live with steady courage under any trial. We understand that while we live in our physical bodies on earth, we are away from the visible presence of Jesus. Our life on earth is only a temporary journey, while heaven is our true home.

Christians guide their daily conduct and choices by faith rather than by what can be seen with physical eyes. To walk by faith means trusting God's promises and living for unseen eternal realities. Even though we cannot see our Savior yet, his truth directs our everyday path.

Paul repeats that believers remain cheerful and bold even when facing danger and death. If given the choice, we would prefer to leave this earthly body behind, because dying brings a Christian straight into the presence of Jesus. Being at home with the Lord is far greater than any joy in this present world.

With such a wonderful future promised to us, our highest goal in life is to please Christ. This ambition applies whether we are still living on earth or already resting in heaven with him. Every day gives us an opportunity to honor our Master through loving obedience.

Every person will one day stand openly before Christ's judgment seat. In ancient cities, this was a raised platform where a judge decided cases or handed out athletic awards. Each person will receive what is due for how they lived in their earthly body, showing whether their deeds were pleasing to God or worthless.

differ.view: Believers stand before this judgment seat only to receive rewards for faithful service, not to face condemnation or punishment for sins, which Christ already washed away.
Even the forgiven sins of believers may be uncovered at this judgment to show the depth of God's mercy and the reality of their repentance, though without shame or condemnation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Every person faces judgment where deeds performed in cooperation with God's grace merit eternal reward, while evil works bring punishment.

notes.meaning: Knowing the reverent awe that belongs to the Lord as Judge, the apostles urge and persuade people to turn to him. Paul's heart and pure motives are already open and clear to God. He hopes the Corinthian believers also recognize his sincere character in their own consciences.

Paul is not trying to praise himself or win popularity. Instead, he gives the Corinthians good facts so they can defend his ministry against false teachers. Those critics boasted about outward things like fancy speech and social standing, but God looks at whether a person has a sincere heart.

Some opponents claimed Paul was crazy because of his extreme zeal and spiritual experiences. Paul answers that if his passionate devotion looks like madness, it is all for God's glory. When he teaches with calm and careful words, it is to build up the believers in their faith.

The driving force behind Paul's tireless work is the love that Christ displayed on the cross. This love holds him to his calling like a strong current. Since Jesus died as a representative substitute for all, all who belong to him are counted as having died to their old, sinful life.

differ.view: Christ died particularly for the elect, who are united to him by God's decree and truly died with him to sin.
Christ died for every single human being without exception, proving that all people were dead in sin and needed his salvation.

notes.meaning: Jesus gave his life for us so that our whole purpose would change. Those who receive spiritual life through him must no longer live selfishly for their own desires, honor, or comfort. Instead, we are called to live for the Savior who died in our place and rose again from the grave.

Christians no longer evaluate other people by worldly standards such as race, wealth, or social rank. Paul once viewed Jesus purely from a human standpoint, seeing him as an ordinary man or a false prophet. Now that his eyes have been opened, he sees Christ as the risen Lord and views all people through the lens of the gospel.

Anyone who is united to Christ by faith is made completely new by God's power. The old life of sin, guilt, and worldly goals has passed away. A fresh life of spiritual renewal and relationship with God has taken its place.

differ.view: Emphasize that the new creation involves an actual moral change in the believer's heart, producing inward holiness and freedom from sin.
Emphasize that being a new creation begins with a believer's spiritual rebirth and legal union with Christ, which then works itself out in renewed living.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The new creation is not just an individual change of heart, but the renewal of the whole world, which Christians enter through baptism and the sacraments.

notes.meaning: This entire new life begins with God and not with human effort. To be reconciled means that two enemies have their broken relationship repaired and restored to peace. God ended our separation by sending Christ to pay for our sins, and he has now given his followers the mission of telling others this good news.

The heart of the gospel message is that God worked through Christ to restore a sinful world to friendship with himself. Instead of holding people's sins against them, God freely offers forgiveness through his Son. He has placed this life-changing message into our hands so we can share it with others.

Believers are official spokespeople, or ambassadors, representing Christ to the world. When the gospel is shared faithfully, it is as though God himself is speaking through human voices. With deep care and urgency, we plead with people to receive God's offer of forgiveness and be made right with him.

Jesus never committed any sin, yet God treated him on the cross as the bearer of our guilt. He took the punishment for our disobedience so that through faith in him we might receive righteousness, which means being counted fully right and accepted before God. This great exchange is the heart of how God saves sinners.

differ.view: Our sins were legally credited, or imputed, to Christ on the cross, and his perfect righteousness is credited to believers by faith alone.
Christ was made a sin offering for us so that God both pardons our guilt and implants actual inward holiness in our hearts through the Holy Spirit.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Christ offered himself as a sacrifice for sin so that believers are not only declared righteous in a legal sense, but are truly transformed and made holy inside by God's grace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Greek wording reflects the ancient Hebrew term for a sin offering, presenting Christ as the sacrificial offering who bore the sins of his people in Isaiah 53.
